name: Jefferson Davis
role: US senator from Mississippi and president of the Confederate States (1861-1865)
summary: Davis was the leading Senate spokesman for slaveholding interests and States' rights, and he led the Confederacy. He defended the right of States to secede and held that the Declaration's equality did not apply to enslaved people, but as wartime president he used conscription, martial law and habeas corpus suspension.

right-to-secede.rationale: In his 1861 farewell to the Senate Davis said secession rests on the sovereignty of each State, which may reclaim the powers it granted, and he concurred in Mississippi's withdrawal.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Davis said Massachusetts would have had the right to leave and he would 'neither vote one dollar nor one man to coerce her back'; he held there were no US laws to execute in a seceded State.

consent-of-governed.rationale: His inaugural address presents secession as an example of the principle that governments rest on the consent of the governed and the right of the people to alter or abolish them.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Davis argued that 'all men are created equal' referred only to the political community, had 'no reference to the slave', and that the Constitution treated enslaved people as a lower caste not equal to white men.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Davis wrote that African servitude 'was in no wise the cause of the conflict, but only an incident', and gave sectional tariff and power conflicts as the causes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Davis called the protective tariffs a sectional grievance that put the main burden of taxation on the South and for the benefit of manufacturers, and praised the Confederate Constitution for prohibiting protective duties.

free-trade.rationale: Davis said the Confederacy's true policy was 'the freest trade which our necessities will permit', and prized free trade between the States, but he did not state the general claim about everyone's long-run benefit.

conscription.rationale: As Confederate president Davis pushed through the first draft in April 1862, according to this reference work.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Davis asked the Confederate Congress in 1864 to suspend habeas corpus against disloyalty and desertion, and as president used martial law and confiscation, according to these reports.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Davis held the Constitution and the courts' reading of it a barrier that bars a national majority from depriving States of their rights, and treated the Dred Scott ruling as binding.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Davis described the Constitution as the 'barrier' protecting a minority from a majority, and the Confederate Constitution he led kept the US guarantees, but he did not discuss a bill of rights as such.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: Davis called nullification peaceful and justified when the federal agent breaks the compact and a State denies its right to act, though he preferred secession.

elective-rulers.rationale: Davis set out the Declaration's principles as that there is no divine right to rule and no man inherits the right to govern.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Davis said that if the Constitution were perverted to destroy the South's rights, the States should redeem them even through revolution, as the colonists did against the Crown.

revolution-justified.rationale: Davis said Southerners would 'redeem our rights even if it be through the process of revolution' if the Constitution were perverted against them, and led Mississippi's and the Confederacy's separation.

political-violence-never.rationale: Davis held that armed revolution to defend the States' rights was justified and led it.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Davis voted repeatedly to take up the bill to facilitate acquiring Cuba by negotiation, and supported Polk's expansion into Oregon and the war with Mexico.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Davis opposed Congress excluding foreign paupers and criminals or limiting immigrants' suffrage, praising the foreign born's labour and blood spent for the country.
